name: Burro
description: Burro (also known as Donkey) is a card game where players try to get rid of all their cards by following suit. The Spanish version uses a 48-card Spanish-suited pack and is closely related to the Indonesian game Cangkul. Players who cannot follow suit must draw from the stock until they find a playable card.

content.text: Burro (also known as Donkey) is a card game where players try to get rid of all their cards by following suit. The Spanish version uses a 48-card Spanish-suited pack and is closely related to the Indonesian game Cangkul. Players who cannot follow suit must draw from the stock until they find a playable card.

Country/Region of Origin: Spain and Portugal
Time Period: Traditional game, documented in 20th century
Historical Development: The game is known as Burro (Donkey) in Spanish-speaking regions. A similar game called Cangkul is played in Indonesia, and Donkey is played in Goa.
Cultural Significance: Popular children's and family game in Spain, Portugal, and Latin America

Minimum Players: 2
Maximum Players: 8
Optimal Players: 4-5
Partnerships: No, each plays for themselves

Type: 48-card Spanish-suited pack
Number of Decks: 1
Card Ranks: King (high), Horse, Maid, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1/Ace (low)
Alternative: 40-card pack (omit 9s and 8s)

48-card Spanish pack (or 40-card)
Score sheet for penalty points
Table space

Cards per Player: 4 cards each
Dealing Pattern: Anticlockwise, one card at a time
Stock: Remaining cards form face-down drawing stock

items.text: Burro with 48-card Spanish pack: Plays with a 48-card Spanish-suited pack ranked King, Horse, Maid, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 in each suit. Four cards are dealt to each player and the remainder form a single face-down stock as described in the Spanish rules.

Burro with 40-card Spanish pack: Uses a 40-card Spanish pack by omitting the 9s and 8s from each suit. The rest of the rules follow the standard Spanish Burro game where players try to shed all cards by following suit and drawing when unable.

Burro Deitado (Portugal): Portuguese children’s version using a 40-card pack where five cards are dealt to each player and the remaining cards form a normal face-down stack. Players are allowed to keep drawing from the stock even if they already hold a playable card of the led suit.

Burro em Pé (Portugal): Portuguese variant where the undealt cards are split into two halves and stood upright in a Λ shape. Players draw from this standing stock and anyone who knocks it over must take all remaining stock cards in addition to normal Burro play.

Burro in Portugal – first out wins: In some Portuguese groups play ends immediately when a player runs out of cards and that player wins, rather than playing multiple hands and scoring penalty points for the last player holding cards.
